papers.title: Biallelic BECN1 variants cause neurodevelopmental disorders via AMPA receptor dysregulation
papers.summary: This study identifies biallelic variants in the BECN1 gene, which encodes Beclin-1, a core autophagy protein, as a cause of neurodevelopmental disorders in affected patients. The researchers show that these mutations disrupt normal autophagy function and lead to dysregulation of AMPA receptors, which are critical for synaptic signaling in neurons. This connects a fundamental cellular clearance pathway to neuronal communication defects, offering a mechanistic explanation for the cognitive and developmental symptoms observed in patients.
papers.why: This paper directly links core autophagy machinery dysfunction to neuronal synaptic signaling defects, providing valuable mechanistic insight relevant to the project's focus on mitophagy/autophagy in neurons and their broader functional consequences in the brain.

papers.title: Mitochondrial protein import stress in Parkinson’s disease: the TOM/TIM–PINK1/Parkin–DELE1/HRI axis linking mitochondrial proteostasis to neuronal death
papers.summary: This paper discusses how stress in importing proteins into mitochondria can trigger a cellular alarm system in Parkinson's disease. It centers on a pathway involving proteins called TOM/TIM, PINK1/Parkin, and DELE1/HRI, which together sense mitochondrial dysfunction and relay that information to the rest of the cell. This signaling can ultimately lead to neuronal death, linking mitochondrial quality control problems to the brain cell loss seen in Parkinson's disease.
papers.why: Since PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy is a core mechanism this PhD project investigates in neurons, understanding the upstream mitochondrial protein import stress response could reveal new regulatory nodes relevant to interneuron vulnerability and degeneration.

papers.title: Ellagitannin Metabolite Urolithin D Ameliorates Cognitive Function and Behavioral Performance in Aging Mice Partially via AMPK/PGC-1α/SIRT3-Dependent Regulation of Mitophagy-Related Molecular Machinery.
papers.summary: This study tests Urolithin D, a metabolite derived from dietary ellagitannins, in aging mice to see if it improves memory and behavior. The researchers found that Urolithin D activates the AMPK/PGC-1α/SIRT3 signaling pathway, which is known to regulate mitochondrial quality control. This pathway activation was linked to enhanced mitophagy, the process by which damaged mitochondria are cleared from cells, correlating with better cognitive outcomes in the aged mice.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it demonstrates a pharmacological route to boost mitophagy in the aging brain via a well-defined molecular pathway, offering a potential therapeutic angle and mechanistic reference point for the project's focus on mitophagy regulation in neurons.

papers.title: Emerging mechanisms of ATG8-independent non-canonical autophagy.
papers.summary: This paper reviews new findings on non-canonical autophagy pathways that operate without requiring the typical ATG8/LC3 lipidation machinery. It likely covers alternative mechanisms by which cells can degrade or recycle cellular components, highlighting newly discovered regulatory proteins and triggers distinct from classical macroautophagy. The review probably discusses how these pathways intersect with membrane trafficking and stress responses in various cell types.
papers.why: Since mitophagy and autophagy in neurons often rely on ATG8-family proteins, understanding ATG8-independent non-canonical autophagy mechanisms could reveal alternative or compensatory pathways relevant to neuronal mitochondrial quality control and interneuron health.

papers.title: Selective autophagy inhibition alleviates oxidative stress-associated neurodegeneration in an AD+CCH model
papers.summary: This study examines a combined Alzheimer's disease and chronic cerebral hypoperfusion (AD+CCH) model, in which the brain experiences both amyloid pathology and reduced blood flow. The researchers found that inhibiting selective autophagy pathways reduced oxidative stress and associated neurodegeneration in this model. This suggests that, in certain disease contexts, excessive or dysregulated autophagy can be harmful rather than protective.
papers.why: This directly relates to selective autophagy/mitophagy dysregulation as a driver of neuronal oxidative damage, a core mechanism of interest for understanding neurodegeneration in the PhD project.

papers.title: Caloric restriction mimetics rewire the AMPK-mTOR-ULK1 signaling nexus to restore autophagic proteostasis in the aging brain.
papers.summary: This paper looks at how caloric restriction mimetics, which are compounds that mimic the effects of calorie restriction, affect brain aging. It focuses on a key cell signaling pathway called AMPK-mTOR-ULK1, which controls autophagy, the process cells use to clean out damaged components. The study suggests these mimetics can restore proper autophagy function in aging brains, improving the removal of unwanted or damaged proteins.
papers.why: Since the project centers on mitophagy and autophagy regulation in neurons, understanding how AMPK-mTOR-ULK1 signaling can be pharmacologically rewired offers potential mechanistic insight and intervention points relevant to neuronal proteostasis research.

papers.title: PDE4D inhibition activates cAMP-PKA signaling to preserve mitochondrial homeostasis and prevent neuronal necroptosis in Alzheimer's disease
papers.summary: This paper investigates how inhibiting an enzyme called PDE4D boosts a signaling pathway (cAMP-PKA) in neurons affected by Alzheimer's disease. This signaling helps maintain healthy mitochondria, the energy-producing parts of cells. As a result, it prevents a type of programmed cell death called necroptosis in neurons, suggesting a potential therapeutic strategy for Alzheimer's.
papers.why: This research connects to the profile's focus on mitochondrial quality control and neuronal survival mechanisms in neurodegenerative disease, relevant to understanding mitophagy dysregulation in the brain.
